extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (graduate students, postdocs, researchers) seeking career/advice on seminars and conferences
extracted.subtask_description: Practical advice for mathematicians (especially early-career) about attending talks and conferences — including talks outside your immediate field — to learn, network, find collaborators, and maintain motivation. Emphasises listening skill and realistic expectations about comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend talks and conferences, even those not directly related to your work
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend talks and conferences even if they are not directly related to your immediate research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern mathematics is collaborative; knowing what others are doing — even in different areas — gives valuable perspectives on your own work. The post's title and opening recommendation stress active participation in the seminar/conference ecosystem rather than strict narrow specialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know what’s going on elsewhere in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to know what’s going on elsewhere in mathematics, and what other mathematicians find interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping informed about other areas often provides valuable perspectives for your own research. This is presented as a substantive criterion for career development and intellectual growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend talks in nearby fields (not just your immediate field)
rubrics_metrics.description: This is true not just for talks in your immediate field, but also in nearby fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure to neighboring fields can introduce techniques, intuition, or viewpoints that are applicable to your problems. The post explicitly recommends branching out to 'nearby fields' rather than only attending hyper-specialised talks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study at different places
rubrics_metrics.description: Study at different places (institutions) to gain broader perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tao recommends studying at different places for much the same reason as attending talks in other fields: to learn diverse techniques, meet people, and gain context that can influence your research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek inspiring talks to boost motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: An inspiring talk can increase your motivation in your own work and in the field of mathematics in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond technical learning, talks can serve to renew enthusiasm and drive; attending inspirational speakers is a legitimate aim of going to conferences and seminars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know who’s who and acquaint yourself with colleagues
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to know who’s who, both in your field and in neighboring ones, and to acquaint yourself with your colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Networking and personal acquaintance prepare you for future collaborations or serendipitous connections when your work becomes relevant to others. Talks and conferences facilitate meeting people and building a professional network.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use talks and conferences to build community and find collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: Talks and conferences are an excellent way to acquaint yourself with your mathematical community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as both a social and strategic criterion: being embedded in the community makes collaborations and awareness of opportunities more likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk to other mathematicians before attempting long isolated work
rubrics_metrics.description: While solitary work can lead to major breakthroughs, such success typically requires first talking to other mathematicians to learn techniques, intuition, and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tao warns that solving major problems in isolation is possible only after one has engaged with others to acquire necessary background; this argues for proactive consultation and exchange rather than pure isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expect to understand 100% of talks outside your field
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t expect to understand 100% of any given talk, especially if it is in a field you are not familiar with; as long as you learn something, the effort is not wasted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set realistic expectations: partial understanding is normal and cumulative — repeated exposure will increase comprehension. The metric of success is learning something, not full comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring your own work to occupy time if not getting much from a talk
rubrics_metrics.description: One can always bring some of your own work to quietly work on once one is no longer getting much out of the talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice for maximizing time at seminars: if the talk ceases to be productive for you, switch to productive solitary work rather than leaving entirely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know how to listen and profit even from poor talks
rubrics_metrics.description: Know how to listen, and you will profit even from those who talk badly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good listening skills can extract value even from poorly delivered talks; Tao also references external resources ('How to listen to a maths lecture' and a conference guide) for more concrete listening strategies and conference behaviour.
